7: each EDI revision hits several interdependent activities at once.
updates do not reach all functions simultaneously; escalation and MOCA depend on individual initiative, with no clear ownership or timelines.
shortages, backlog, excess stock and obsolescence, sharpest in the move to mass production.

How can Procurement, Production Planning, and Capacity Management be better coordinated to manage EDI demand variability and limit the resulting risks of material shortages, production backlog, and material obsolescence?
How does information flow between functions?
8: From observation to a structured research project
Identify the operational and organizational difficulties of EDI demand changes and propose an integrated approach to cross-functional coordination
Understand how increases and decreases affect decisions · identify coordination difficulties · connect demand information with materials, suppliers, schedules and capacity
Academic: a context-specific coordination framework for pre-series to mass production.  Practical: a structured model for cross-functional decisions at K&S
9: Constructivism, mixed methods and an action-research logic
Meaning is built through practitioners’ interpretation: Planning and Procurement read the same EDI change differently
Embedded single-case study: K&S, Mercedes-Benz VAN program
Qualitative and quantitative evidence combined, not run in parallel
Diagnose, build a provisional model, refine with practitioners; agreement is not proof of improvement
10: Two evidence streams: ten voices and the company’s own records
Purposive sample; experience from about 1.5 to 14 years
Interview guide adapted to each function
Field notes: daily replanning, procurement escalation meetings
EDI call-off overviews: demand variability (Release CW28 vs CW29)
Excel weekly plans and requirement lists: customer requirement (LAB) vs confirmed plan (VSAT)
ERP/Krosy reports: cross-check of backlog and material coverage
Qualitative + quantitative evidence  →  TRIANGULATION  →  a fuller understanding of the coordination problem

15: Three lenses on the same problem
No single best structure: coordination must fit the environment and its uncertainty.
So: different responses to increases and decreases
Sensing → Seizing → Transforming: detect change, act on it, renew routines.
So: detect, decide and adapt, not just react
EDI is an enabler; value depends on turning information into coordinated action.
So: align information, responsibilities and decisions
Context: ramp-up and pre-series logistics require coordinated capacity, materials and information flows before series production (Filla & Klingebiel 2014; Wlazlak et al. 2018; Wochner et al. 2016)
